familiarityAgeDesc.message: How long ago your first recorded visit was. A domain registered last week can't clear this one at all.

Off, they come one per line, as “Visits: 3”, and the bar each one has to clear is one hover away. showWarningNotificationDesc.message: Warnings appear only on unfamiliar sites, and only during the interactions chosen below. Nothing is shown while you're simply reading a page.

browserNotificationsDesc.message: System notifications, shown outside the page. Nothing on the page can touch them, but your operating system can silence them, for example in do-not-disturb mode, and they're easy to miss while you're looking at another window.

inPageNotificationsDesc.message: A panel drawn on the page itself. Your system can't silence it and it's hard to miss, but it lives inside the page, so a hostile site can try to remove it. Catching that is what the tamper protection below is for.

notificationStylePinNote.message: As you can see, every style has a caveat of its own. That's why pinning the extension icon to the toolbar is worth doing. The icon sits in the browser's own frame, outside every page, so a site can neither silence it, nor remove it, nor draw a convincing fake over it. Whatever happens to a notification, the icon still tells you how well the site is known.
notificationStylePinNote.description: Note below the notification style options, recommending the pinned icon as the indicator a site cannot fake

importHistoryRunDesc.message: Runs the same two passes the automatic import ran. First the summary the browser keeps for each page, which brings visit counts up to date in a moment. Then every recorded visit, one page at a time, which is the only place first-visit dates and active days can come from – slower on a large history, and you can cancel at any point without losing what it has already read. Worth running if the automatic import didn't finish, or if history has synced in from another device since. Safe to repeat: counts are matched, not added up.

That resemblance is what Visilant is here to catch, so it keeps no count for names like localhost and never warns about them. None of this is a verdict on the machine itself, only on what an address alone can tell you.

showInputWarningDesc.message: Typing and pasting is the moment your data actually leaves your hands. A fake login page can't take anything until you fill it in, so this is the last point at which a warning can still stop a password, a card number or a one-time code from going to the wrong site.

The common trick is a site that asks you to copy a line and paste it into a terminal or a run box, and what actually landed in the clipboard is malicious code rather than the harmless line you saw on screen. A warning here gives you a reason to look at it once more before pasting.

Allowing it doesn't paste anything by itself: you press paste again and it goes through as an ordinary paste, with formatting, images, undo and the page’s own handling all behaving normally. After that the page stops asking.

punycodeHelpContent.message:
Punycode is a technical format for domains with special characters. It starts with 'xn--'.

Potential Risk:
The danger arises when a domain looks like it only contains standard English letters (ASCII), but is actually Punycode. This usually means it contains hidden 'look-alike' characters from other languages to impersonate a trusted site.

If the domain characters are in the same language as the website content, then Punycode is expected and likely safe.

linkShortUrlSectionWarning.message: Resolving a shortened link means actually requesting it and following every hop to the end. Each host along the way sees that request, the final destination included, so it learns your address and that someone followed the link. It's still far less exposure than opening the page, because nothing is rendered and no script on it ever runs, but it isn't nothing: a click can be counted, a one-time link can be spent, and a server can act on the request. If a link looks suspicious, not resolving it at all is the safer choice.

emailCaveatLinks.message: A link or a QR code out of the message can be pasted into the field above, and it's worth doing when the link claims to be somewhere you already use. Whether it really is that site is the one question this extension can answer. A name you've never seen before it can't judge at all, and neither can you by looking, so put that one through {virustotal-url} or {urlscan} instead.

emailCaveatAttachments.message: Attachments are a different matter: ask someone you trust if you have anybody to ask, and otherwise send the file to {virustotal-file} rather than opening it. If you're in doubt, don't download it at all – some file types can do harm before anyone opens them.

welcomeTitle.description: Title of the welcome page shown right after install

welcomeSubtitle.message: One thing was set up for you.

welcomeWhyTitle.description: Heading of the section explaining why the history was imported

welcomeWhyBody.message: Visilant decides what to warn about by comparing a site against the ones you already use. With nothing to compare against it can't tell your bank from a copy of it, so on an empty profile it either stays quiet when it shouldn't, or flags everything in sight. A warning that appears on every site is a warning you stop reading – and by the time a genuinely dangerous one turns up, it looks exactly like the harmless ones before it. Reading your history once, up front, is what makes the difference between the two mean something.
welcomeWhyBody.description: Explanation of why the history import happens automatically

welcomeStatusReading.description: Shown while the browser history is being read

welcomeStatusSaving.description: Shown while the imported sites are being saved

welcomeStatusDone.message: Visilant now knows how often you've been to each of these sites. The ones you use regularly won't be warned about. New and rarely visited ones still will be.
welcomeStatusDone.description: Shown under the import result numbers. The numbers count every site read from the history, familiar or not, so this must not call them all familiar: only the ones that pass the familiarity rules are.

welcomeStatusFailed.message: The import didn't finish, so Visilant still treats every site as new. You can run it again.
welcomeStatusFailed.description: Shown when the automatic import failed

welcomeStatusCancelled.message: The import was stopped before it finished. You can run it again.
welcomeStatusCancelled.description: Shown when the import was stopped before finishing

welcomeStatusUnsupported.message: This browser keeps its history to itself, so there was nothing to import. Visilant learns your sites as you visit them, and until it has seen a site it will call it unfamiliar.
welcomeStatusUnsupported.description: Shown when the browser has no history API, as on Firefox for Android

welcomeDetailsRunning.message: Your sites are counted. Now filling in first-visit dates and active-day counts. Until that's done, sites you know may still be warned about.
welcomeDetailsRunning.description: Shown while the slower detail pass of the import is still running. The counting pass stores visits only, and the shipped familiarity rules also need active days and a first visit, so until this pass lands no imported site is familiar yet.

welcomeKeepOpen.message: Carry on browsing as usual and feel free to close this page – the import runs in the background. Just try not to close the browser itself until it's done. If you do, it saves its place as it goes and picks up where it left off next time you start the browser.
welcomeKeepOpen.description: Hint shown while the import runs, about keeping the browser open

welcomeTabDone.description: Tab title flashed when the import finishes while the user is on another tab

welcomeDetailsFailed.message: The extra pass that fills in first-visit dates and active days didn't finish. Your sites are counted, but until those are in, sites you know may still be warned about.
welcomeDetailsFailed.description: Shown when the detail pass failed but the counting pass succeeded. Without its dates a site fails the active-day and first-visit checks, which the shipped rules require, so warnings do not yet know the imported sites.

welcomeRetry.description: Label of the button that runs the import again

welcomeStatSites.description: Unit under the number of imported sites

welcomeStatVisits.description: Unit under the number of imported visits

welcomeSavedTitle.description: Heading of the list of what the import stored

welcomeSavedHostname.message: the host name of the site, such as example.com
welcomeSavedHostname.description: First item of what the import stored

welcomeSavedCount.message: how many times you've been there
welcomeSavedCount.description: Second item of what the import stored

welcomeSavedFirstSeen.message: the date of your earliest recorded visit
welcomeSavedFirstSeen.description: Item of what the import stored: the first visit date

welcomeSavedLastSeen.description: Third item of what the import stored

welcomeSavedActiveDays.message: how many separate days you visited it on
welcomeSavedActiveDays.description: Item of what the import stored: the number of active days

welcomeSavedRetention.message: These numbers only reach as far back as the browser’s own history does. Browsers drop old entries after a while on their own, so a site you've used for years can show far fewer visits and a much later first visit than you'd expect. That's the browser’s retention setting rather than a miscount. It also explains why a site you've known for years, but visit rarely, can fall short of the familiarity threshold and trigger a warning. From here on Visilant keeps its own count and misses none of your visits. It simply can't look backwards, so a gap like that belongs to the early days and closes as you browse.
welcomeSavedRetention.description: Note that the imported numbers only reach as far back as the browser keeps history

welcomeSubtitleNoImport.message: Nothing was read, and nothing had to be.
welcomeSubtitleNoImport.description: Subtitle of the welcome page on a browser that does not share its history

welcomeWhyTitleNoImport.description: Heading of the first welcome section on a browser with no history API

welcomeWhyBodyNoImport.message: Visilant decides what to warn about by comparing a site against the ones you already use. Here there was nothing to start from, so it begins knowing nothing at all. That's worth knowing up front, because for the first while it will call sites unfamiliar that you've used for years – including your bank and your mailbox. It isn't wrong, it simply hasn't seen them yet. Every visit teaches it one, and the warnings thin out on their own.
welcomeWhyBodyNoImport.description: Body of the first welcome section on a browser with no history API

welcomeSavedTitleNoImport.message: What it records as you browse
welcomeSavedTitleNoImport.description: Heading of the data section on a browser with no history API

welcomeSavedNoImportNote.message: From the first time you open a site, and never anything from before that.
welcomeSavedNoImportNote.description: Line under the recorded-data list on a browser with no history API

welcomeNotSavedTitle.description: Heading of the paragraph listing what is not stored

welcomeNotSaved.message: Page addresses, page titles, search queries and anything you've typed aren't stored. Only the five things above, per host name.
welcomeNotSaved.description: What the import deliberately does not store

welcomeStorageTitle.description: Heading of the section about where the data lives

welcomeStorageBody.message: In this browser’s own storage, on this device. Visilant has no server and no account, and none of it is ever sent anywhere. You can erase all of it at any time in the settings.
welcomeStorageBody.description: Statement that the data stays on the device

welcomeOpenSettings.description: Label of the welcome page button opening the settings

welcomeDone.description: Label of the welcome page button closing the tab

welcomeDefaultsTitle.description: Heading of the section suggesting a look at the settings

welcomeDefaultsBody.message: The defaults are meant to suit most people, but they were picked by one person, largely around how that person browses. Visilant collects no telemetry – there's no way to see how anyone else has things set, and so no way to know what a better default would even be. Spend a couple of minutes in the settings: what warns you, when, and how loudly is all adjustable, and reading through it is also the fastest way to understand how the extension works.
welcomeDefaultsBody.description: Why the defaults are a guess and worth reviewing

familiarityNoImportText.message: sites have no active-day count and no first-visit date. This browser keeps its history to itself, so there's no import that could fill them in and those two checks will keep failing for them. Only the visit count still speaks for these sites. Everything you visit from now on records both from its first visit.
